claims.text: A controlled Nb-Mo-Ta-W-Zr elemental powder mixture with O, N, and C each below 500 ppm and D50 of 20-45 µm is a suitable initial feedstock.
Selective Laser Melting can fabricate a Nb-Mo-Ta-W-Zr refractory high-entropy alloy from the proposed powder feedstock.
SLM power above 300 W, scan speed above 800 mm/s, and energy density of 80-100 J/mm³ are appropriate processing conditions for this alloy.
Solution annealing at 1400°C for 1 hour under pressure below 10^-5 Pa, followed by aging at 1100°C for 30 minutes and rapid quenching, is an effective post-processing route.
The proposed SLM and heat-treatment route will produce a microstructure dominated by a BCC solid-solution matrix.
The BCC matrix will contain a high density of coherent nanoscale B2 precipitates enriched in Nb and Ta.
Rapid solidification and dynamic recrystallization during annealing will refine the grain size to below 5 µm.
Rapid solidification during SLM traps interstitial impurities in the lattice and prevents their segregation to grain boundaries.
Solution annealing at 1400°C dissolves brittle TCP phases and homogenizes the Nb-Mo-Ta-W-Zr alloy.
Short aging at 1100°C precipitates coherent B2 particles without forming large brittle intermetallics.
The coherent B2 precipitates impede dislocation motion through Orowan strengthening.
A continuous BCC matrix containing discrete coherent precipitates can preserve high strength while improving ductility relative to an ordered continuous matrix.
The refined grains and coherent precipitates collectively increase alloy strength.
Suppressing interstitial segregation at grain boundaries mitigates brittleness.
The processed alloy will have a yield strength above 800 MPa at 1000°C.
The processed alloy will exhibit room-temperature tensile elongation above 10%.
Conventionally cast or slowly cooled Nb-Mo-Ta-W-Zr alloys typically form brittle Laves or sigma phases, have coarse grains, and exhibit room-temperature ductility below 2%.
The proposed alloy will significantly outperform conventionally cast or slowly cooled Nb-Mo-Ta-W-Zr counterparts.
The strategy applies to equiatomic or near-equiatomic Group IV-V refractory alloys but may fail with significant Group III or VI additions.
Interstitial contents above 1000 ppm overwhelm the proposed trapping mechanism.

contradictions.description: The microstructure is called single-phase BCC while also being specified to contain B2 precipitates; a BCC matrix plus a distinct B2 precipitate population is a two-phase microstructure.
The boundary excludes alloys with significant Group VI additions, but the proposed alloy itself contains Mo and W, both Group VI elements, as principal constituents.
